newsitem.title: UK: Britain to act over public sector strikes - union.
newsitem.headline: Britain to act over public sector strikes - union.

text.p: The British government is planning a new anti-union law to allow members of the public to sue unions in the public sector for any serious inconvenience caused by strikes, the Trades Union Congress (TUC) said on Friday.
The plans, leaked to the TUC, Britain's main union umbrella body, follow government warnings of new legislation after strikes disrupted post and rail services this summer.
"This is a cynical bit of pre-election politics, but the government has seriously misunderstood the mood of the public," TUC general secretary John Monks told a press briefing.
He said recent surveys showed Britons were more concerned about "job insecurity and over-mighty bosses" than strikes.
The number of days lost through strikes has gone up this year, but from a low base -- days lost in 1994 were at an historic low, and the 1995 figure was not much higher.
A series of anti-union laws enacted by the Conservative government since 1979, coupled with high unemployment, have curbed union militancy.

Among the new proposals, the government says unions should be liable to legal action and claims for damages from any member of the public or company where a public sector strike has a "disproportionate or excessive effect".
At present, unions enjoy immunity from claims as long as members have voted for a strike in a ballot.
The TUC said the proposal was "confused and unrealistic" and would clog up the courts.

"Every passenger on a cancelled train would have to bring a court case," a spokesman said. In addition, a union would have no way of knowing in advance of strike action what was legal and what might have "excessive" effects, he said. Among the other proposals, the government wants the notice period -- or cooling-down period -- for union action after members vote for a strike to be doubled to 14 days from seven.

It also says strikes should be voted for by a majority of those entitled to vote rather than a majority of those voting, as at present. The TUC said its leaked copy suggested the proposals would be published on Monday, but a spokeswoman for the Department of Trade and Industry denied this. Either way, TUC officials said there was little prospect of the plans becoming law before the next election, which must be held by May 1997.
